_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. status: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, cite in note), 'provisional' (my romanization, not found outside; builder marks it), 'decided' (a project style call). Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored.

郁慕俠.cast: The author: a Shanghai newspaperman of the 1920s-30s, whose beat was the treaty-port city's low life and slang.
郁慕俠.note: Pen name of the journalist and tabloid (xiaobao) writer who compiled these sketches; the surname is Yu (郁). Active in the Shanghai small-paper press of the 1920s and 1930s.

天虛我生.note: The pen name of Chen Diexian (陳蝶仙, 1879–1940), a prolific novelist of the “Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies” school, editor of the Shenbao’s literary supplement, and industrialist who founded Household Industries (家庭工業社), maker of Butterfly-brand toothpowder. He wrote this preface.

南京路.note: The premier commercial street of the International Settlement; older English “Nanking Road.”

南市.note: The old walled Chinese city of Shanghai and the district around it, south of the foreign concessions.

城隍廟.note: The temple of the city's tutelary god (chenghuang) in the old Chinese city; the Shanghai City God Temple and the bazaar around it were a great popular resort.

虹廟.note: A popular temple on (East) Nanjing Road, properly the Bao’an Situ Temple (保安司徒廟), enshrining Guanyin; famous for its dense incense-smoke, and much frequented by Shanghai courtesans.

西湖.note: The famous scenic lake at Hangzhou.

金陵.note: Jinling, a classical name for Nanjing, capital of the Nationalist government from 1927.

租界.note: The foreign-administered concession areas of Shanghai — chiefly the International Settlement and the French Concession — each with its own council, police, and by-laws.

捕房.note: A police station of the concession forces (the Settlement’s Municipal Police, or the French Concession police).

探捕.note: A plain-clothes detective or constable of the concession police.

錢莊.note: A traditional Chinese money-shop or bank (qianzhuang), as distinct from the foreign banks; the mainstay of Chinese commercial credit.

國曆.note: The Gregorian (solar) calendar, adopted by the Republic on 1 January 1912 as the guoli, “national calendar.”

陰曆.note: The traditional lunisolar calendar (also called the old calendar, jiuli), which set the dates of the traditional New Year and festivals.

財神.note: The god of wealth, welcomed into shops and homes at the New Year to secure a prosperous year of trade.

接路頭.note: The Shanghai term for welcoming the God of Wealth; lutou (“road-head”) is the local name of the god. Kept on the night of the fourth day of the first month.

元宵.note: The fifteenth of the first lunar month, the last day of the New Year season.

元旦.note: Here the first day of the first lunar month — the traditional New Year — not the Gregorian 1 January.

菩薩.note: In popular speech any temple god or idol, not only a Buddhist bodhisattva.

小洋.note: Subsidiary silver coin (dimes and twenty-cent pieces), which passed at a slight discount to the standard silver dollar (dayang).

元寶茶.note: New Year tea served with two olives on the lid, the olives standing for silver ingots (yuanbao) — an auspicious wish for wealth.

壓歲錢.note: New Year money given by elders to children, “to weigh down the year” (and, by a pun on sui, to ward off evil); the Shanghai word in the text is yasui dian (壓歲鈿), dian being the Wu-dialect word for money.
